title: Every Great Developer Sells One of Four Things
summary: The firms people call elite are not doing one mysterious thing. Each runs one of four business models, and each model earns its money from a different pocket and carries a different risk. Learn to name the model before you copy any of its habits.
body:
Every developer, contractor or wealth builder you admire is running one of four business models, and each one gets paid from a different pocket. Copy a habit without knowing which model it belongs to, and you inherit the risk without the reward.

Recall

Q. What is a board's first job in a growing development company?

A. To oversee the people who run it: approve strategy and major decisions, test the numbers, and hold management to account. A board that only signs what it is shown is decoration.

Q. When you compare hold, sell and refinance, what must every option be measured on?

A. After-tax cash to the owner, on the same timeline and the same assumptions, so the options are compared like for like.

Q. What is the danger of a change made after design sign-off?

A. It can travel into the building without the engineer of record re-checking the whole design, which is how small changes become structural failures.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week we reverse engineer the people at the top of your field. The temptation is to collect their habits like souvenirs: one firm's monthly reporting, another's lean overhead, a third's appetite for size. That is how small developers get hurt. A habit is a part of a machine. Lifted out of its machine and bolted into yours, it can do the opposite of what it did for them. So before any habit, we name the machine.

The four models

In plain English: there are four ways to make money from buildings, and most famous names are known for one of them.

The first is the merchant builder: buy land, get approvals, build, sell, and move to the next site. The money comes from the development spread, the gap between what the building costs and what a buyer pays for it. The second is the long-term owner: build or buy, then hold for decades and collect rent. The money comes from income and from value growing slowly over time. The third is the fee developer, sometimes called the developer-manager: the firm puts up a small slice of the equity, raises the rest from institutions, and earns fees for developing and managing the asset plus a promote, a share of profit above an agreed return. The money comes from other people's capital. The fourth is the integrated builder-developer: a construction company that also develops, using the steady cash a contracting business generates to fund its own projects.

The professional framing is that each model has a different engine and a different weak point. The merchant builder's engine is turnover; its weak point is a market that stops buying halfway through a project. The long-term owner's engine is compounding; its weak point is debt that comes due before the income can carry it. The fee developer's engine is scale on borrowed trust; its weak point is reputation, because one bad fund closes the door on the next. The integrated builder's engine is construction cash flow; its weak point is that construction margins are thin and one bad contract can drain the cash the development side depends on.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. One project costs 40,000,000 dollars all in. As a merchant builder you sell it on completion for 46,000,000 dollars. After selling costs of about 1,000,000 dollars, profit is 5,000,000 dollars, earned once, taxed once, and then you need another site. As a long-term owner, the same building produces net operating income (NOI), the rent left after operating costs and before debt and tax, of 2,600,000 dollars a year. You earn nothing on day one, but you keep a growing income and the building itself. Same bricks, two different businesses.

Say that out loud now.

Merchant builders earn the spread once. Owners earn the income for decades. Fee developers earn on other people's money. Integrated builders fund development with construction cash.

How the best do it

Some examples where the facts are well established. Brookfield, a Canadian-headquartered firm, combines two roles: it owns real assets with its own capital and it manages capital for institutional investors, earning fees on that capital. Bechtel has been privately owned by one family since its founding, which lets it take a long view on very large engineering and construction projects without answering to public shareholders each quarter. Turner, a large American construction manager, is owned by the German group HOCHTIEF. And the great landed estates of London, such as the Grosvenor family's holdings in Mayfair and Belgravia, show the long-term owner model at its purest: land held across generations and income taken from leases rather than from sales.

What a small developer can copy is not their size. It is their clarity. Each knows which engine it runs and builds its controls around that engine's weak point. Brookfield-style owner-managers keep their own capital in the deals they manage, so their incentive and their investors' point the same way. Family-owned builders keep decision-making close and fast. Long-term estates refuse to sell good land to fund a bad year.

Mixing models on purpose

Most mature firms mix models, but they mix them deliberately. A second worked example, hypothetical. You raise 18,000,000 dollars of equity from an institution for a 45,000,000 dollar project, and put in 2,000,000 dollars yourself. You charge a development fee of 3 percent of cost, about 1,350,000 dollars, which is a fee-developer pocket. You keep a 10 percent ownership share, which is an owner pocket. If the deal beats an agreed return, you earn a promote, which is the fee developer's real prize. Three pockets on one project. The discipline is to know which pocket pays your overhead this year, which builds your net worth, and which is a hope. On Day 5, Sage works the full arithmetic.

Marco's point on delivery belongs here. A fee developer that also controls construction has a conflict: the investor wants the lowest sensible cost and the builder wants the best margin. The firms that handle this well price their own construction against the market, disclose the relationship and let the investor test it. The firms that do not, eventually lose the investor.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: fees, ownership profit and promote can be taxed differently, and the difference depends on local law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: managing other people's money brings duties to them that owning your own does not. Banking: lenders size and price each model differently, and a merchant builder's corporate credit looks nothing like a long-term owner's. Governance: a mixed model needs written rules for conflicts between your pockets. Estate: a portfolio of held buildings passes to heirs; a stream of fees usually dies with the key person. Exit: merchant builders exit every project; long-term owners may never exit, so the exit is the succession plan.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer and tax adviser, before you set up any structure that earns fees on other people's capital.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is copying the growth of a model without copying its funding. A long-term owner borrowing short-term money to build like a merchant has neither model's protection. The control is a one-line statement in your business plan naming your model, its engine and its weak point, reviewed before every new project.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner admires the biggest name in the room and assumes its methods suit a firm of any size. Size is an output of a model run well for decades. Copy the discipline, not the scale.

Callback

In Week 1, Remi described the developer's job as a lifecycle with value levers and go/no-go gates. The four models are four different decisions about where on that lifecycle you take your money out: at completion, through income, through fees, or through construction. The gates stay the same in every model. What changes is which gate pays you.

Recap

There are four models: merchant builder, long-term owner, fee developer and integrated builder-developer. Each has an engine and a weak point. Elite firms know which they run and build controls around the weak point. Copy their discipline, not their size.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Olympia and York, an elite developer whose model outran its money.
checklist: I can name which of the four models my next project uses.
I can state that model's engine and its weak point in one sentence each.
I know which pocket pays my overhead this year.
I know which pocket builds my net worth over time.
Any habit I copy from a large firm, I first trace back to its model.
My funding term matches the time my model needs to repay it.
I have written rules for conflicts between my own pockets.
head: Field checklist
speak: There are four ways to make money from buildings. The merchant builder buys land, builds and sells, and earns the development spread once. The long-term owner holds for decades and earns income and slow value growth. The fee developer puts up a small slice of equity, raises the rest from institutions and earns fees plus a promote, a share of profit above an agreed return. The integrated builder-developer uses construction cash flow to fund its own projects. Each model has an engine and a weak point: turnover and a stalled market; compounding and debt due too early; scale on trust and a damaged reputation; construction cash and one bad contract. The firms people call elite know which model they run and build their controls around its weak point. So before I copy any famous firm's habit, I name the model it belongs to. I copy the discipline, not the size.
terms: Merchant builder — a developer who builds to sell and earns the gap between cost and sale price.
Fee developer — a developer who earns fees and a share of profit for developing and managing projects funded mostly by other investors.
Promote — the sponsor's share of profit above its share of capital, paid only once investors clear an agreed return.

hostile.q: You say you want to be a long-term owner, but your plan sells every building you finish. Which are you?
hostile.a: Today I am a merchant builder, because I need the spread to build equity, and I am saying so plainly. My plan names the point at which I begin holding: when retained profit can fund the equity in a held building without short-term debt. Until then I will not borrow short to hold long, because that combination has neither model's protection.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on risk and the lender's view
title: Olympia and York 1992: An Elite Model That Outran Its Money
summary: Olympia and York was among the most admired developers in the world before it sought creditor protection in 1992. Its buildings were good; its funding did not match the time those buildings needed. Seven steps take the case apart and produce Rule 129.
body:
Olympia and York was an elite developer by any measure, and it still failed. The buildings were not the problem. The problem was money that came due faster than the buildings could pay it back.

Recall

Q. What is key-person risk in a development company?

A. The danger that the business, its relationships or its loans depend on one person, so that losing that person damages the company. Lenders and investors test for it.

Q. Why can a refinance look better than a sale on a spreadsheet?

A. Because refinance proceeds are borrowed, not earned, and often carry no immediate tax, while the new debt and its risk are easy to leave out of the comparison.

Q. What is a hold point in a quality plan?

A. A stage beyond which work may not proceed until a named person inspects and releases it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week is about learning from the best. A failure case belongs here because even the best can fail, and the way they fail tells you which part of their model you must never copy carelessly. Roman sits with me today because the root cause is financial.

Step 1: the timeline

Olympia and York was a family-controlled Canadian developer, run by the Reichmann brothers from Toronto. Through the 1970s and 1980s it built a reputation for large, high-quality office developments in Toronto and New York, including the World Financial Center at Battery Park City in Manhattan. In the late 1980s it committed to Canary Wharf, a very large new office district in London's Docklands, then far from the established financial centre. The property market in London and North America weakened sharply at the start of the 1990s. In May 1992 Olympia and York sought protection from its creditors in Canada and the United States, and Canary Wharf was placed into administration in the United Kingdom. Canary Wharf later succeeded as a business district, under new ownership.

Step 2: the key decisions

Three decisions stand out. First, building a whole new district at Canary Wharf largely on the firm's own balance sheet, including major infrastructure costs that a private developer rarely carries. Second, funding the group substantially with shorter-term borrowing, including bank loans and short-term debt raised in markets, against assets that would take many years to lease up. Third, keeping the group private and closely held, which concentrated decisions and limited the outside scrutiny that might have questioned the funding profile.

Step 3: the assumptions

The central assumption was that a firm with this track record could always refinance. A related assumption was that tenants would follow quality and that the transport links Canary Wharf needed would arrive in time. Underneath both was the assumption that the market cycle would hold long enough for the new district to fill. Each was reasonable in a good year. None was tested against a bad one.

Step 4: the incentives

Lenders were keen to lend to a famous name, which lowered the price and raised the volume of short money available. Success had rewarded boldness for two decades, so the internal incentive was to keep doing what had worked. And a privately held firm answered to its owners, who had every reason to believe in their own record.

Say that out loud now.

A strong track record makes short money cheap, and cheap short money is exactly what a long project should refuse.

Step 5: the warning signs ignored

Roman's view: the warning signs were structural rather than secret. The office market in London was softening as Canary Wharf rose. The transport links were not yet in place. Debt maturities were stacked closer together than the leasing timetable. A worked example of the shape, with hypothetical round numbers. A group holds buildings that will produce stable income in seven years. It borrows 1,000,000,000 dollars, of which 400,000,000 dollars must be repaid or refinanced within 18 months. In a good market, refinancing is routine. In a falling market, lenders shrink, values fall, and the group must find 400,000,000 dollars from buildings that are not yet earning. The building did not change. The money did.

Step 6: the point of no return

The point of no return came when the cost of finishing and holding Canary Wharf could no longer be funded without new borrowing, at the same moment the market for that borrowing closed. After that, every option involved the creditors deciding the outcome. A second hypothetical worked example shows why the moment matters. With two years of liquidity, a developer can wait out a downturn that lasts eighteen months. With six months of liquidity, the same downturn ends the firm. Liquidity is the length of the storm you can survive.

Step 7: the root cause

The root cause was a mismatch of duration: long-life assets that needed many years to earn their income, funded in significant part by money that had to be repaid or replaced in a short time. Everything else, the market, the transport delays, the size of the bet, turned a manageable risk into a fatal one because the funding could not wait.

What the patient version would have looked like

Reverse engineer the case and ask what funding would have survived. Roman's answer has three parts, none of them exotic. First, long-term loans for long-term buildings: debt whose maturity sits after the date the building is expected to be leased and earning, with extension options that the borrower can exercise as of right if defined tests are met. Second, phasing: build the district in stages, so each stage is funded and leased before the next is committed, and a downturn stops the next stage rather than threatening the ones already built. Third, shared infrastructure: the roads, transit and public realm that a new district needs are usually funded with public partners or by agreement with the authorities, because they serve far more than one owner's buildings.

A hypothetical comparison makes the trade visible. A developer can build four office towers at once on short money and save perhaps two years of construction time. Or it can build two, lease them, refinance them on long terms and then build the next two. The second path earns less in a strong market and survives a weak one. Elite firms with long lives tend to choose the second path more often than their reputations suggest. Patience is not timidity. It is a funding decision.

The prevention rule

Rule 129: Never copy an elite developer's ambition without its funding: match the term of every dollar to the time the asset needs to pay it back, and hold enough liquidity to outlast a downturn without asking anyone's permission.

This is a fact pattern drawn from widely reported events; treat the details as a teaching summary and read the primary accounts before you cite them in a meeting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing your reputation is collateral. It is not. When the market turns, lenders lend against cash flow and value, and a famous name refinances no faster than a careful one. The control is a maturity schedule that sits beside every leasing schedule, with no maturity earlier than the income that must repay it, plus a stated liquidity floor in months.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears that a great firm failed and concludes it was unlucky or reckless. It was neither. It was a sound developer running a funding structure that only worked if the cycle cooperated. The lesson is not to be timid. It is to be patient with your money.

Callback

In Week 45, Nadia and Priya taught exit financing: the refinance, the take-out and the maturity gap. Olympia and York is that maturity gap at the scale of a whole company. The questions you learned to ask of one loan, when is it due and what repays it, are the questions to ask of every loan in a group at once.

Recap

Olympia and York was admired and well run, and its buildings proved good. It failed because long-life assets were funded with money that came due too soon, in a cycle that turned. Rule 129: match the term of the money to the time the asset needs, and hold liquidity to outlast a downturn.

Next: Warrick on The Money: how the four models fill a personal balance sheet differently.
checklist: I keep a maturity schedule beside every leasing schedule.
No loan in my plan matures before the income meant to repay it.
I have stated my liquidity floor in months, not dollars.
I do not treat my reputation as collateral.
I test every plan against a downturn that lasts longer than my liquidity.
Large infrastructure costs are either shared or funded with patient money.
I read primary accounts before citing a failure case in a meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: Olympia and York was a family-controlled Canadian developer, admired for large, high-quality office buildings in Toronto and New York. In the late 1980s it committed to Canary Wharf, a new office district in London. The market weakened in the early 1990s, and in May 1992 the group sought creditor protection, and Canary Wharf went into administration. The buildings were not the root cause. The root cause was duration: long-life assets that needed years to lease up, funded in large part by money that had to be repaid or replaced quickly. A famous name made short money cheap, and in a falling market that money could not be replaced. Liquidity is the length of the storm you can survive. Rule 129: never copy an elite developer's ambition without its funding. Match the term of every dollar to the time the asset needs to pay it back, and hold enough liquidity to outlast a downturn.
terms: Duration mismatch — funding long-life assets with money that must be repaid or replaced over a much shorter period.
Liquidity floor — the minimum cash and committed funding held, measured as months of obligations it can cover.
Administration — a United Kingdom insolvency process in which an appointed administrator runs a company for its creditors.

hostile.q: Your portfolio has two loans maturing next year and your new building will not stabilise for three. How is that different from Olympia and York?
hostile.a: In shape it is not different, which is why I am fixing it before I commit. I will either extend both maturities past stabilisation now, while the market is open, or hold committed liquidity covering both repayments. I will not start the new building until one of those is done, and I will show you the maturity schedule beside the leasing schedule so you can check that no loan comes due before the income that repays it.

rule: Rule 129: Never copy an elite developer's ambition without its funding: match the term of every dollar to the time the asset needs to pay it back, and hold enough liquidity to outlast a downturn without asking anyone's permission.

title: Three Pockets: Fees, Ownership and Promote
summary: Each business model pays its owner through a different mix of three pockets: fees, ownership returns and promote. They differ in certainty, timing and tax character, and they build a personal balance sheet in very different ways. Learn to value each pocket separately.
body:
A developer is paid from up to three pockets: fees, ownership returns and promote. They look like one income on a summary page, but they differ in how certain, how early and how taxed they are, and only one of them reliably builds lasting wealth.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between management and a board in a growing company?

A. Management runs the business day to day. The board oversees management, approves major decisions and holds it to account.

Q. Why should hold, sell and refinance be compared after tax?

A. Because the tax on each option arrives at a different time and in a different amount, and the comparison that ignores it can choose the wrong option.

Q. What is a contractor's collapse risk on a project?

A. The chance that the contractor becomes insolvent mid-project, leaving unfinished work, unpaid subcontractors and liens, usually worsened by front-loaded payments.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the firms we studied on Day 1 differ most in where their money comes from. When you build your own company you will choose a mix. The mix decides how steady your income is, how much risk sits on your personal balance sheet and what you leave behind. Today we price each pocket.

Pocket one: fees

In plain English: fees are money you are paid for work, whether or not the deal succeeds.

The professional framing: development fees, asset management fees and construction management fees are paid from the project or from investors' capital, usually as a percentage of cost or of equity. These percentages are commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal, not standards. Fees are the most certain pocket and the earliest, which is why they pay overhead. They are also usually taxed as ordinary business income in the year earned, and they rarely survive your departure, because an investor pays fees for your work, not for your name on a share register. Tax treatment depends on local law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. You earn a 3 percent development fee on a 45,000,000 dollar project, about 1,350,000 dollars over three years, so about 450,000 dollars a year. Your company's overhead, staff, office and pursuit costs on dead deals, is 400,000 dollars a year. Fees cover overhead with about 50,000 dollars left. That is a safe year, not a wealthy one. Fees keep the lights on.

Pocket two: ownership

In plain English: ownership returns are what your own invested money earns, the same as any other investor.

The professional framing: when you co-invest, your share of distributions is pro rata to your capital. It is less certain than fees and arrives later, at stabilisation, refinance or sale. Its great advantage is that it is an asset. Ownership sits on your balance sheet, can be held for decades, borrowed against carefully and passed on. It is the pocket that compounds.

Say that out loud now.

Fees pay the overhead. Ownership builds the balance sheet. Promote is the upside I do not spend before it arrives.

Pocket three: promote

In plain English: promote is your extra share of profit when the deal beats the investors' required return.

The professional framing: the promote, also called carried interest in fund language, is paid only after investors receive their capital back and a preferred return, an agreed minimum annual return. It is the least certain pocket and the latest, and it is often exposed to clawback, a requirement to return promote already paid if later results fall short. It can be very large. It is also the pocket that beginners spend in their heads before it exists.

A second worked example, hypothetical. On the same project, you put in 2,000,000 dollars of equity and the deal is expected to earn you about 2,060,000 dollars of profit including roughly 960,000 dollars of promote. Now haircut each pocket for certainty, a habit, not a formula. The fees, already contracted, you count at full value. The ownership profit, if the market holds, you might count at 80 percent. The promote, which depends on beating the hurdle, you might count at 50 percent. The deal that looked like 3,410,000 dollars of total reward, fees plus profit, is worth something closer to 2,710,000 dollars when you discount each pocket for its own risk: 1,350,000 dollars of fees, about 880,000 dollars of ownership profit and about 480,000 dollars of promote. That gap is the size of the mistake you avoid by not adding the pockets together.

Matching the pockets to the models

The merchant builder lives mostly on ownership profit, earned once per project, with no recurring fees. The long-term owner lives on ownership income that compounds. The fee developer lives on fees and hopes for promote, with a small ownership slice that aligns it with investors. The integrated builder lives on construction margin, a fee-like pocket, and reinvests it in ownership. Each mix has a different picture of risk. A fee-heavy firm has steady income but little to leave behind. An ownership-heavy firm has a strong balance sheet but uneven cash and more debt to manage.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, only ownership shows up as an asset you own. Fees become cash, which you can save but which stops when the work stops. Promote shows up as nothing until it is paid, and then as cash and a tax bill. So the ledger question for any business model is: how much of what I earn each year is converted into ownership I keep? A firm that earns large fees and spends them on lifestyle has an income, not wealth. A firm that turns a fixed share of every fee and every promote into retained ownership is building an estate. Decide that share in writing before the money arrives. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal investment decision.

A ten-year ledger, hypothetical

Picture two developers who each earn 500,000 dollars a year of fees after tax and overhead for ten years, and each receive one promote of 1,000,000 dollars after tax in year six. The first spends all of it as it arrives. At the end of year ten he has a good reputation, a comfortable decade and almost nothing that produces income without his work. The second sets a rule in year one: half of every fee and all of every promote goes into ownership, his co-investment in the deals he manages. That is 250,000 dollars a year plus the 1,000,000 dollar promote, a total of 3,500,000 dollars of ownership put to work over the decade, before any growth on it. If those stakes earn a modest return, he finishes year ten owning pieces of buildings that pay him whether or not he works next year.

Both men had the same income. Only one built wealth. The difference was not skill or luck. It was a written conversion rule, set before the money arrived, and followed when it was tempting not to. The numbers are illustrative; the habit is the point.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing your company on its promote. A firm that hires, borrows and spends as if every deal will clear its hurdle is one weak cycle from crisis. The control is a budget in which fees alone cover overhead, and promote is planned only after it is paid and taxed.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner adds fees, profit and promote into one number and calls it what the deal makes. Value each pocket separately, at its own certainty, and on its own date.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX and Elias taught the waterfall: preferred return, catch-up, promote and clawback, and the tax character of developer fees. Today put that machinery on your own balance sheet. The waterfall decides when each pocket is paid. The ledger decides which pocket is still there in twenty years.

Recap

A developer is paid in fees, ownership and promote. Fees are certain and early and pay overhead. Ownership is uncertain but compounds and can be passed on. Promote is the least certain and the latest. Value each separately, cover overhead with fees alone, and convert a fixed share of every pocket into ownership.

Next: Omar on The Rules: the governance that keeps a fee model honest, with a Canada and Guyana comparison.
checklist: I value fees, ownership and promote separately, each at its own certainty.
My company's overhead is covered by fees alone.
I do not plan spending around promote that has not been paid.
I know whether my promote is exposed to clawback.
I have decided in writing what share of every fee and promote becomes retained ownership.
I check the tax character of each pocket with an adviser before relying on it.
I know which mix of pockets my business model depends on.
head: Field checklist
speak: A developer is paid from up to three pockets. Fees are paid for work, whether the deal succeeds or not. They are certain and early, usually taxed as income, and they pay the overhead, but they stop when the work stops. Ownership is what my own invested money earns. It arrives later and is less certain, but it is an asset I keep, can hold for decades and pass on. Promote is my extra share of profit above the investors' preferred return. It is the least certain and the latest, often subject to clawback. So I never add the three into one number. I value each at its own certainty and date. On my balance sheet, only ownership is wealth; fees are income and promote is nothing until paid. My rules are that fees alone cover overhead, promote is planned only after it is paid and taxed, and a fixed share of every fee and promote becomes ownership I keep.
terms: Preferred return — an agreed minimum annual return that investors receive before the sponsor shares in profit.
Clawback — a requirement for the sponsor to return promote already paid if later results fall short of the agreed hurdle.
Co-investment — the sponsor's own capital invested in a deal alongside its investors, on the same terms.

hostile.q: Your company budget assumes promote income in year three. What happens if the deal misses its hurdle?
hostile.a: You are right to ask, and the budget should not depend on it. I am rebuilding it so that contracted fees alone cover overhead in every year, and promote appears only as a possible addition after it is paid and taxed. If the hurdle is missed, the company is still solvent; the shortfall falls on my upside, not on my staff or my lenders.

title: Governing a Fee Model: Conflicts, Disclosure and Removal
summary: When a developer manages other people's money, the law and the contracts add duties that a developer investing alone never faces. The best firms make conflicts visible, cap related-party dealing and accept that investors can remove them. Learn the governance and a conceptual Canada and Guyana comparison.
body:
The moment you earn fees on other people's capital, you are no longer only an owner. You are a manager with duties, and the best firms in the world earn trust by writing those duties down before anyone asks.

Recall

Q. In Week 128, what does a board resolution do?

A. It records a decision of the board in writing, so that the company's authority to act is clear and can be shown to a lender, auditor or court.

Q. What is the difference between a sale and a refinance for tax purposes, in concept?

A. A sale is generally a disposition that can trigger tax on a gain. A refinance is borrowing, which generally is not income, though rules vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is a bypassed hold point?

A. Work that continued past a required inspection without the named person releasing it, so defects were covered up before anyone checked them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the fee-developer model studied on Day 1 is how many small developers grow, because it lets you build more than your own capital allows. It is also where most of the legal risk of growth sits. You will be deciding things that spend other people's money, sometimes in ways that pay you. That combination is exactly what governance exists to control.

The duties that arrive with other people's money

In plain English: when you manage money for others, you must put their interests ahead of your own in the areas you control, and you must tell them about anything that could tempt you not to.

The professional framing: depending on the structure and the jurisdiction, a manager or general partner may owe fiduciary duties, which are duties of loyalty and care, or contractual duties defined in the partnership or operating agreement, or both. Many agreements narrow or define these duties, and the law in some places limits how far they can be narrowed. Whether a duty exists and how far it reaches is a legal question for your counsel, not a matter of commercial preference. Offering interests to investors can also bring securities rules into play, as Weeks 70 and 71 explained in concept.

The governance tools the best firms use are consistent. Conflicts are disclosed in writing. Related-party transactions, any deal between the venture and the manager or its affiliates, need investor approval or an independent check. Fees are defined precisely, with no fee charged twice on the same work. Investors receive regular reports in an agreed format. And investors can remove the manager, for cause and sometimes without cause, on terms set in advance.

Related-party dealing: the conflict that ends funds

A worked example, hypothetical. You manage a joint venture that needs a general contractor. Your own construction company bids 30,000,000 dollars. Two outside contractors bid 29,000,000 and 31,000,000 dollars. Hiring your company may be perfectly fair, but the investor cannot know that from your say-so. A well-written agreement requires you to disclose the relationship, provide the competing bids, cap your company's fee at a stated percentage, give the investor's representative audit rights over the construction accounts, and obtain written approval before award. If the investor approves, you have a relationship you can defend. If you skip those steps, a later cost overrun looks like self-dealing even if it was bad luck.

Say that out loud now.

A conflict I disclose and an investor approves is a relationship. A conflict I hide is a liability waiting for a bad quarter.

Fee offsets and removal

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your agreement pays you a 1 percent annual asset management fee on 20,000,000 dollars of equity, so 200,000 dollars a year. You also receive a 50,000 dollar acquisition fee from a broker on a property the venture buys. A fee-offset clause, common practice in institutional deals, requires that fees you receive from third parties in connection with the venture reduce the fees the venture pays you. Here the asset management fee for that year would fall to 150,000 dollars. The clause exists because an investor does not want you paid twice for one deal. The percentages are commercial practice and vary; your agreement decides.

Removal terms are the other half. Investors usually can remove a manager for cause, such as fraud, wilful misconduct or a material breach, and the agreement defines each term. Some agreements also allow removal without cause by a supermajority vote, usually with a payment to the departing manager. The important document is the one written before trouble: what happens to your promote, your fees and your co-investment if you are removed. Negotiate that when you are trusted, not when you are under review.

A removal clause, read slowly

Take a hypothetical clause and read it the way an investor's counsel would. "The Manager may be removed for Cause by notice from Investors holding a majority of the Interests. Cause means fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence or a material breach not cured within 30 days of notice. On removal for Cause, the Manager forfeits any unpaid Promote." Three questions sit in it. Who decides that cause exists, the investors alone or a court or arbitrator? Is gross negligence defined, or will it be argued about? And what happens to the manager's co-investment: is it bought out, and at what value?

Now the version without cause. "Investors holding 75 percent of the Interests may remove the Manager without Cause on 90 days' notice, on payment of accrued fees and the Promote that would be payable on a sale at appraised value on the removal date." This protects you, because removal without cause carries a price. The percentages, notice periods and valuation method are commercial practice and are negotiated; your counsel decides what is enforceable. The habit to learn is reading each defined term and each consequence, not just the headline right.

Two Systems

Canada and Guyana both draw heavily on English common law, so the ideas of fiduciary duty, partnership and the enforceability of a negotiated agreement are familiar in both. Canada's company and partnership law is set provincially and federally, and its securities regulation is largely provincial, with each province and territory having its own regulator. Guyana has its own companies and partnership legislation and a single national securities regulator. In both systems, the agreement you sign does much of the work, but statute can impose duties the agreement cannot remove. This is a conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source and local counsel in each country before relying on it. [unverified — confirm independently]

Professional sign-off required: corporate and securities lawyer in each jurisdiction, before you accept investor money or sign any related-party contract.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating governance as paperwork that slows you down. The first time an investor discovers an undisclosed conflict, the question stops being whether you built a good building and becomes whether you can be trusted with their money. The control is a written conflicts register, reviewed at every investor report, with every related-party contract approved in writing before award.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes a friendly investor will not mind a family company doing the work or a small extra fee. Friendly investors become strict investors the day a project goes over budget. Write the rules while everyone is friendly.

Callback

In Week 68, JAX taught investor and joint venture governance: major decisions, reporting and alignment. Today adds the edge cases that end relationships: related-party contracts, duplicate fees and removal. The major-decisions list from that week is where most of these protections are written, so read the two lessons together.

Recap

Managing other people's money brings duties of loyalty and care, defined by law and by the agreement. The best firms disclose conflicts, get approval for related-party deals, offset duplicate fees and agree removal terms in advance. Canada and Guyana share common-law roots but differ in statute and regulators; verify both.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: the full arithmetic of a sponsor's three pockets on one hypothetical project.
checklist: I keep a written conflicts register for every venture I manage.
Every related-party contract is disclosed, competitively tested and approved in writing before award.
My agreements define each fee precisely and include a fee-offset clause.
I know the removal terms, for cause and without cause, in every agreement I manage.
I know what happens to my promote, fees and co-investment if I am removed.
I have securities and corporate counsel in each jurisdiction before accepting investor money.
I report to investors in an agreed format on an agreed schedule.
head: Field checklist
speak: When I earn fees on other people's capital, I become a manager with duties, not just an owner. Depending on the structure and the law, those can be fiduciary duties of loyalty and care, contractual duties, or both, and some cannot be removed by agreement. The best firms make conflicts visible. They disclose them in writing, get approval for any related-party deal, such as hiring their own construction company, offset fees received from third parties so they are not paid twice, report on a fixed schedule, and agree in advance how investors can remove them. I negotiate the removal terms while I am trusted, not when I am under review. Canada and Guyana both draw on English common law, but their statutes and securities regulators differ, so I verify both with local counsel. A disclosed, approved conflict is a relationship. A hidden one is a liability waiting for a bad quarter.
terms: Fiduciary duty — a legal duty to act loyally and carefully in another person's interest in matters you control for them.
Related-party transaction — a deal between a venture and its manager or the manager's affiliates.
Fee offset — a clause that reduces the fees a venture pays its manager by fees the manager receives from third parties in connection with the venture.

hostile.q: Your own company is the contractor, the developer and the asset manager. Why should I believe I am getting market terms?
hostile.a: You should not take my word for it, and the agreement does not ask you to. Every related-party contract comes to you with competing bids, a capped fee, audit rights over the accounts and a written approval before award. Third-party fees I receive reduce the fees you pay me. And you can remove me for cause on defined terms. If any of those protections is missing from the draft, I will add it.

title: The Sponsor's Three Pockets, Worked Step by Step
summary: A worked calculation of one hypothetical fee-developer project: the waterfall, the promote, the fees and the sponsor's total return. The numbers show why a small equity slice can produce a large return, and why that return depends on clearing the hurdle.
body:
A fee developer can earn a large multiple on a small cheque, but almost all of the extra comes from clearing the investors' hurdle. Work the waterfall step by step and you can see exactly where the sponsor's return is earned and where it can vanish.

Recall

Q. What are the three pockets a developer can be paid from?

A. Fees for work, ownership returns on the developer's own invested capital, and promote, a share of profit above the investors' required return.

Q. When comparing a hold with a sale, what is the danger of using a refinance number?

A. Refinance proceeds are borrowed, so treating them as profit overstates the return and hides the new debt.

Q. In a construction post-mortem, what usually turns a contractor's difficulty into a collapse?

A. Payments that ran ahead of work in place, leaving no cushion when the contractor's cash ran out.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an institutional partner will ask you to show your economics line by line. If you cannot work this waterfall yourself, you cannot negotiate it, and you cannot tell whether the promote you are offered is generous or empty. All figures today are hypothetical round numbers. Fee levels, preferred returns and splits are commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal, not standards.

Step 1: the deal

A project costs 50,000,000 dollars. Debt funds 30,000,000 dollars. Equity is 20,000,000 dollars: an institution puts in 18,000,000 dollars, which is 90 percent, and you, the sponsor, put in 2,000,000 dollars, which is 10 percent. The waterfall is simple, with no catch-up, so the arithmetic stays visible: first, all equity gets its capital back; second, all equity gets an 8 percent preferred return, compounded annually; third, everything left is split 80 percent to the equity holders in proportion to capital and 20 percent to you as promote.

The project is sold at the end of year 4. After repaying the loan and paying selling costs, 32,000,000 dollars is left for the equity. To keep the example clean, assume no distributions before the sale.

Step 2: return of capital

The first 20,000,000 dollars goes back to the equity in proportion: 18,000,000 dollars to the institution and 2,000,000 dollars to you. Remaining: 32,000,000 less 20,000,000 equals 12,000,000 dollars.

Step 3: the preferred return

Eight percent compounded for four years on 20,000,000 dollars. Multiply 1.08 by itself four times: 1.08, 1.1664, about 1.2597, about 1.3605. The accrued preferred return is 20,000,000 dollars times 0.3605, which is about 7,210,000 dollars. In proportion, about 6,489,000 dollars goes to the institution and about 721,000 dollars to you. Remaining: 12,000,000 less 7,210,000 equals about 4,790,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Capital back first, then the preferred return, then the split. The promote lives only in what is left after the hurdle.

Step 4: the split and the promote

Of the remaining 4,790,000 dollars, 20 percent is your promote: about 958,000 dollars. The other 80 percent, about 3,832,000 dollars, is shared in proportion to capital: about 3,449,000 dollars to the institution and about 383,000 dollars to you.

Check the total. The institution receives 18,000,000 plus 6,489,000 plus 3,449,000, about 27,938,000 dollars. You receive 2,000,000 plus 721,000 plus 383,000 plus 958,000, about 4,062,000 dollars. Together, about 32,000,000 dollars. The waterfall balances, which is the first thing any partner will check.

Step 5: the fees

Now add the fee pocket. You earned a development fee of 3 percent on 45,000,000 dollars of hard and soft costs, about 1,350,000 dollars, and an asset management fee of 1 percent of equity a year, 200,000 dollars for four years, so 800,000 dollars. Total fees: about 2,150,000 dollars. These were costs of the project, already inside the 50,000,000 dollars, which is why they are not deducted again here.

Step 6: the scorecard

The institution invested 18,000,000 dollars and received about 27,938,000 dollars, an equity multiple of about 1.55 times. You invested 2,000,000 dollars and received about 4,062,000 dollars from the waterfall, a multiple of about 2.03 times on your capital, plus about 2,150,000 dollars of fees. Including fees, about 6,212,000 dollars came to you against a 2,000,000 dollar cheque. Your return is far higher than the institution's, and the reason is visible: the promote and the fees.

Worked example two: the deal that misses

Now run it again with 26,000,000 dollars left for equity instead of 32,000,000 dollars. Capital back takes 20,000,000 dollars, leaving 6,000,000 dollars. The preferred return owed is about 7,210,000 dollars, so the hurdle is not cleared. All 6,000,000 dollars goes to the preferred return in proportion: 5,400,000 dollars to the institution and 600,000 dollars to you. No split, no promote. You receive 2,600,000 dollars from the waterfall, a multiple of 1.3 times, plus the same 2,150,000 dollars of fees. A drop of 6,000,000 dollars in the proceeds left for equity, about 19 percent, cut your waterfall cash by about 1,460,000 dollars, about 36 percent. The promote is a lever, and levers work in both directions.

Step 7: find the promote-zero line

Every partner will ask where your promote disappears, so calculate it before they do. The promote begins only after capital and the compounded preferred return are paid. In this deal that is 20,000,000 dollars of capital plus about 7,210,000 dollars of preferred return, about 27,210,000 dollars. Below that amount of equity proceeds, your promote is zero. Above it, every additional dollar pays you 20 cents of promote plus your 10 percent share of the other 80 cents, about 8 cents, so about 28 cents in total.

Translate that into the property. If the loan payoff and selling costs are fixed, the equity proceeds move one for one with the sale price. The base case delivered 32,000,000 dollars to equity, so the sale price can fall by about 4,790,000 dollars before your promote reaches zero. On a building selling for, say, 64,000,000 dollars, that is a fall of about 7.5 percent. That one number, the percentage drop in value that wipes out your promote, tells you and the investor how much of your reward is genuine margin and how much is a bet on the market holding.

Reading what the numbers say

Three lessons sit in this table. First, your fees were the same in both cases, which is why fees pay overhead. Second, your promote disappeared entirely in the second case, which is why promote is never budgeted. Third, the institution's return fell much less than yours in percentage terms, because the waterfall puts the investor first. That ordering is exactly what you are selling to an institution: you take the risk on the upside so they are protected on the downside.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting the base-case promote as your expected income. It is a contingent claim that disappears at a modest shortfall. The control is to show every partner, and yourself, the waterfall at three outcomes: base, downside and the point where the promote reaches zero.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets that the preferred return compounds, works it as simple interest, and overstates the promote. Here simple interest would give 6,400,000 dollars instead of about 7,210,000 dollars, an error of about 810,000 dollars, and about 162,000 dollars of promote that would never be paid.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught levered and unlevered returns, the equity multiple and the traps in an internal rate of return. Today's two scorecards are that lesson applied to the sponsor's seat: the same project produced a 1.55 times multiple for the investor and a much higher one for you, and the difference is structure, not skill.

Recap

Run the waterfall in order: capital back, compounded preferred return, then the split. The sponsor's outsized return comes from promote and fees. Fees survive a weak result; promote does not. Always show the waterfall at base, downside and the point where promote reaches zero.

Next: JAX on The Room: proposing a programmatic joint venture to an institutional investment committee.
checklist: I can work a waterfall in order: capital, preferred return, split.
I compound the preferred return, never treat it as simple interest.
I check that every waterfall balances to the cash available.
I show partners the waterfall at base, downside and promote-zero outcomes.
I know my equity multiple with and without fees.
I never budget promote as expected income.
I state that fees, preferred returns and splits are commercial practice.
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is a hypothetical fee-developer deal. Equity is 20,000,000 dollars: 18,000,000 from an institution and 2,000,000 from me. After the sale, 32,000,000 dollars is left for equity. First, capital back: 20,000,000. Second, an 8 percent preferred return, compounded over four years, about 7,210,000. Third, the remaining 4,790,000 splits 80 percent to equity in proportion and 20 percent to me as promote, about 958,000. The institution gets about 27,938,000, a 1.55 times multiple. I get about 4,062,000 from the waterfall, about 2.03 times, plus 2,150,000 dollars of fees. Now drop the proceeds to 26,000,000. The hurdle is not cleared, the promote vanishes, and my waterfall cash falls about 36 percent while the proceeds fell about 19 percent. So fees pay overhead, promote is a lever that cuts both ways, and I always show the waterfall at base, downside and the point where promote reaches zero.
terms: Equity multiple — total cash returned to an investor divided by the cash it invested.
Hurdle — the return investors must receive before the sponsor's promote begins.
Compounding — earning a return on a return, so each year's growth is calculated on the larger, accrued balance.

hostile.q: Your base case gives you three times your money including fees. Why should my investment committee accept 1.55 times?
hostile.a: Because the structure puts you first. You get your capital and a compounded 8 percent before I see any promote. In the downside case, where proceeds fall about 19 percent, my promote disappears and you still receive your capital and most of your preferred return. My fees cover real work at commercial rates, and I have disclosed them. If you want more of the upside, we can discuss a higher hurdle or a lower promote, and I will show you each version at base and downside.

title: Pitching a Programmatic Partnership to an Investment Committee
summary: A realistic scene: a small developer proposes a programmatic joint venture to an institutional investor's committee. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question and when to stay silent. A monthly thread on personal brand closes the lesson.
body:
An institution does not fund the building in front of it. It funds the developer it will still trust after the third building. Your job in the committee room is to show you are the kind of partner whose next deal is less risky than this one.

Recall

Q. In Rule 129, what must match?

A. The term of every dollar and the time the asset needs to pay it back, with enough liquidity to outlast a downturn.

Q. In a hold, sell or refinance meeting, what is the question behind a lender's question about a cash-out refinance?

A. Whether the sponsor is taking money out because the building is strong or because the sponsor needs cash elsewhere.

Q. After a construction failure, what is the first thing an owner should secure?

A. The site, people's safety and the records: drawings, inspection reports, change orders and correspondence, before anyone revises them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is how the fee-developer model begins: not with a fund, but with one institution agreeing to back a series of projects. A programmatic joint venture is an agreement in which an investor commits to fund several projects with one sponsor, under common terms, each project still approved separately. It is the bridge between doing deals one at a time and running a platform. Here is the meeting.

Scene one: the opening

Five people from the investor sit across the table: the head of real estate, two analysts, a risk officer and someone from legal. The head of real estate says: "We liked your last project. Tell us why we should commit to a programme rather than look at each deal as it comes."

The question behind the question: is this sponsor asking for a commitment because it is good, or because it cannot raise money deal by deal?

Say: "Because a programme lowers risk for you as well as for me. You get first look at every deal that fits an agreed strategy, common legal terms, one reporting format and a team you already know. I get speed and the ability to commit to land with confidence. Each project still comes to you for separate approval, and you can say no to any of them."

Never say: "We have more deals than we can fund." That sentence tells them your discipline depends on their money.

Scene two: the economics

An analyst asks: "Your fee load looks high. Walk us through it."

Say: "Development fee of 3 percent of hard and soft costs, asset management at 1 percent of equity, and a promote of 20 percent above an 8 percent compounded preferred return. Our co-investment is 10 percent of equity, on the same terms as yours. Third-party fees offset our fees. Here is the waterfall at base, downside and at the point where our promote reaches zero."

Then stop. Let them read the page. Silence is the most credible thing you can offer after a number.

A worked number to have ready, hypothetical. On a 50,000,000 dollar project with 20,000,000 dollars of equity, fees are about 2,150,000 dollars over four years. If the analyst says that is 10.75 percent of their equity, agree: "Yes, roughly 10.75 percent of equity over the life of the project, all inside the budget, and disclosed. In return the team carries the land risk, the entitlement risk and the cost of dead deals, which you never see."

Say that out loud now.

Scene three: the risk officer

The risk officer asks: "What happens to this programme if you are hit by a bus?"

The question behind the question: is this a company or a person?

Say: "A fair question for a firm our size. Three answers. First, a named second person who knows every project and has signing authority under our board resolutions. Second, key-person insurance that funds the transition. Third, your rights: if the key-person event happens and you are not satisfied with the successor within an agreed period, you may suspend new commitments and replace us as asset manager on existing projects on pre-agreed terms."

Never say: "Nothing is going to happen to me." It answers a governance question with a mood.

Scene four: the hard one

Legal asks: "Your construction company will build these projects. How do we know you will not overcharge us?"

Say: "You will not have to trust us. Every construction contract comes to you with competing bids, a capped fee and audit rights over our books, and you approve it in writing before award. If you prefer an outside contractor on any project, we will run that tender."

A second worked number, hypothetical. If your company's bid is 30,000,000 dollars against outside bids of 29,000,000 and 31,000,000 dollars, show all three. Do not explain away the cheaper bid. Say what you offer for the 1,000,000 dollar difference, such as a shorter schedule or a guaranteed maximum price, and let them decide.

Scene five: the close and the follow-up

The head of real estate ends with: "We need to take this to our full committee. What would you need from us to keep working on your next site?"

The question behind the question: will this sponsor pressure us for a fast answer, and will it keep its discipline while it waits?

Say: "Nothing today. I would ask for a decision timeline, so I know whether to hold the next site for you or for my own balance sheet. If your committee has questions, I would rather answer them in writing than have them guessed at."

Never say: "Another investor is very interested." If it is true, they will hear it soon enough from the market. If it is not, they will find out, and the rest of your pitch is discounted.

Then follow up within one business day with a short note: what was agreed, what you owe them, the date each item will arrive and the name of the person on your side for each. Send exactly what you promised, on the date you promised. Institutions often decide on the second meeting based on how the first meeting's promises were kept.

Holding your state

Institutions test composure deliberately. The risk officer's question is not rude; it is the job. Keep your voice at the pace you opened with, answer the bus question in the same tone as the fee question, and write down anything you promise. Close by reading back what you owe them and when: "The key-person clause and the three-case waterfall by Friday."

Personal brand, a monthly thread

Your personal brand, in an institutional room, is not your logo or your social media. It is the record of what you said you would do and whether you did it. Committees keep notes. The developer who sent the promised document on Friday, and whose downside case turned out to be honest, is the one who gets the second programme.

So build the brand you want deliberately: publish nothing you would not defend in this room, keep a log of every commitment made in a meeting and the date you met it, and let your third project's report be as clear as your first pitch.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a programme on terms that let the investor control your pipeline without committing to fund it: exclusivity for you, no obligation for them. The control is to trade exclusivity only for real commitments, such as a target amount of capital, a decision timeline for each deal and a release if they decline a set number of fitting deals.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to fill every silence and ends up negotiating against himself. After you give a number, stop talking.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught interests versus positions and the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. The institution's interest here is reliable deal flow with protection; yours is speed and certainty. A programme works when both interests are written into it, and your alternative, raising deal by deal, is what lets you walk away from bad exclusivity.

Recap

Pitch a programme as lower risk for both sides. State fees precisely and show the waterfall at three outcomes. Answer key-person and related-party questions with mechanisms, not reassurance. Stay silent after numbers. Trade exclusivity only for commitment.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill for elite models.
checklist: I can explain why a programme lowers risk for the investor as well as for me.
I can state my fee load precisely and as a percentage of the investor's equity.
I bring the waterfall at base, downside and promote-zero outcomes.
I have a key-person answer with a named successor, insurance and investor rights.
Every related-party contract comes with competing bids and audit rights.
I trade exclusivity only for real funding commitments.
I keep a log of every commitment made in a meeting and the date I met it.
head: Field checklist
speak: In the investment committee, I pitch a programmatic joint venture as lower risk for both sides: first look at deals in an agreed strategy, common terms, one reporting format and a team they know, with each project still approved separately. I never say I have more deals than I can fund. I state the fees precisely, a 3 percent development fee, 1 percent asset management, and a 20 percent promote above a compounded 8 percent preferred return, with a 10 percent co-investment on the same terms and third-party fees offset. Then I stop and let them read the waterfall at base, downside and promote-zero. When the risk officer asks about the bus, I answer with a named successor, key-person insurance and their right to suspend or replace. When legal asks about my construction company, I offer competing bids, a capped fee, audit rights and written approval. And I trade exclusivity only for real commitment.
terms: Programmatic joint venture — an agreement under which one investor funds a series of a sponsor's projects on common terms, each still approved separately.
Exclusivity — a promise to offer fitting deals to one investor first or only.
Key-person clause — terms that give investors rights if a named individual leaves, dies or is incapacitated.

hostile.q: If we give you a programme, you will stop shopping your deals. What stops you sending us the weak ones?
hostile.a: Three things. First, you approve each project separately and can decline any of them. Second, I co-invest 10 percent on the same terms, so a weak deal costs me before it costs you. Third, my promote only pays above your compounded preferred return, so a weak deal pays me fees and nothing more. I would also accept a clause that releases you from the programme if two approved projects miss their downside case.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 129 Review: Elite Models Reverse Engineered
summary: Six questions test the week: the four models, Olympia and York and Rule 129, the three pockets, governance of a fee model, the waterfall and the investment committee. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical term sheet and a two-minute boardroom drill close the week.
body:
The week came down to one sentence: name the model before you copy the habit, fund it with money as patient as the asset, and govern other people's money as if they were watching, because they are.

Recall

Q. What are the three pockets a developer is paid from?

A. Fees, ownership returns and promote, each with its own certainty, timing and tax character.

Q. What should a hold, sell or refinance decision always be compared on?

A. After-tax cash to the owner, on the same timeline and assumptions for every option.

Q. What is the lesson of a bypassed hold point?

A. Work covered before inspection hides defects, so no named hold point may be passed without the named person's release.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sit across from institutions, partners and lenders who already run one of these models. If you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can hold that conversation as someone who chose his model rather than drifted into it. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four business models and the weak point of each.

Answer: Merchant builder, weak when the market stops buying mid-project. Long-term owner, weak when debt comes due before income can carry it. Fee developer, weak when reputation is damaged. Integrated builder-developer, weak when thin construction margins drain the cash development needs.

Question 2. What was the root cause of Olympia and York's collapse, and what is Rule 129?

Answer: A duration mismatch: long-life assets funded substantially by money due much sooner, in a cycle that turned. Rule 129: never copy an elite developer's ambition without its funding; match the term of every dollar to the time the asset needs, and hold liquidity to outlast a downturn.

Question 3. Which pocket builds lasting wealth, and why?

Answer: Ownership, because it is an asset that can be held, borrowed against carefully and passed on. Fees stop when the work stops, and promote is nothing until paid.

Question 4. Your construction company wants to build a project you manage for an investor. What must happen?

Answer: Disclose the relationship, provide competing bids, cap the fee, give audit rights and get written approval before award.

Question 5. In a waterfall with an 8 percent compounded preferred return over four years on 20,000,000 dollars, what is the accrued return?

Answer: About 7,210,000 dollars, because 1.08 to the fourth power is about 1.3605. Simple interest would wrongly give 6,400,000 dollars.

Question 6. What should you trade for exclusivity in a programmatic joint venture?

Answer: Real commitments: a target amount of capital, a decision timeline for each deal and a release if the investor declines a set number of fitting deals.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Remi named the four models and what a small developer can copy from the best. Ford and Roman took Olympia and York apart and produced Rule 129. Warrick valued fees, ownership and promote separately and set the ledger rule. Omar covered conflicts, related-party dealing, fee offsets, removal and a Canada and Guyana comparison. Sage worked the waterfall at two outcomes. JAX ran the investment committee.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical term sheet extract and find the defects before reading on.

Programme Term Sheet, Draft 2. (1) Sponsor shall offer all residential projects to Investor on an exclusive basis for five years. Investor may accept or decline each project. (2) Preferred return: 8 percent per annum. (3) Promote: 20 percent of profits. (4) Sponsor's affiliate shall act as general contractor on all projects. (5) Sponsor shall receive a development fee of 3 percent, an asset management fee of 1 percent and any acquisition or financing fees customary in the market. (6) Sponsor co-investment: at Sponsor's discretion. (7) Key person: not applicable.

The defects. First, clause 1 gives five years of exclusivity with no investor commitment, no decision timeline and no release; the sponsor's pipeline is controlled by a party that need fund nothing. Second, clause 2 does not say whether the preferred return compounds, from what date, or on what balance; on 20,000,000 dollars over four years the difference between simple and compounded is about 810,000 dollars. Third, clause 3 says 20 percent of profits without saying after what: it should be 20 percent of distributions above capital and the preferred return. Fourth, clause 4 makes the affiliate contractor automatically, with no bids, cap, audit rights or approval. Fifth, clause 5 defines neither fee base, cost or equity, and the phrase customary fees invites fees with no offset. Sixth, clause 6 leaves co-investment optional, which removes alignment. Seventh, clause 7 omits a key-person provision for a firm that depends on one person; the investor's risk officer will strike it first.

The lesson is not that the sponsor drafted badly on purpose. It is that every vague clause is resolved later, usually in favour of whoever is stronger at the time.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to a partner who asks: "What should we copy from the big developers?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Not their size. Their clarity. Every elite firm runs one of four models: build and sell, build and hold, develop with other people's capital for fees and promote, or use construction cash to fund development. Each has a weak point, and the best firms build controls around it. Olympia and York shows what happens when a great developer funds long buildings with short money: Rule 129, match the term of the money to the asset. For us, the likely path is a fee-developer model with a co-investment. That pays us in three pockets. Fees cover overhead, ownership builds wealth, and promote we never budget. Taking other people's money brings duties, so we disclose conflicts, test related-party contracts and agree removal terms in advance. A sample waterfall shows our promote vanishes if the building sells for about 7.5 percent less than plan, which is exactly the risk an institution wants us to carry."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the four models and Rule 129? Did you separate the three pockets? Did you mention governance? Did you finish in two minutes? If not, record again tomorrow.

Where to go back

If Question 1 was slow, reread Day 1 and say the four models aloud with their engines and weak points until you can do it in thirty seconds. If you missed the root cause in Question 2, reread Day 2 and Week 45 together, because the maturity gap is the same idea at two scales. If Question 3 was shaky, reread Day 3 and write your own conversion rule: what share of every fee and promote becomes ownership. If Questions 4 or 6 were vague, reread Day 4 and Day 6, and practise the related-party answer until it comes out as a list of mechanisms rather than a reassurance. If Question 5 was wrong, work the compounding by hand: 1.08, 1.1664, 1.2597, 1.3605, then multiply by the equity.

A second worked check, hypothetical, to test yourself on the Red Pen. If clause 3 had read 20 percent of profits and the deal made 12,000,000 dollars of profit over capital, the sponsor might argue for 2,400,000 dollars of promote. Under the waterfall Sage worked, the correct promote was about 958,000 dollars. That gap of about 1,440,000 dollars is what two missing words, above the preferred return, are worth.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is admiring a model without pricing its weak point. The control is to write your model, engine and weak point on the first page of your business plan.

The beginner's mistake

Signing a term sheet because the headline numbers, 8 percent and 20 percent, look normal. The definitions behind them decide who gets paid.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught what binds in a term sheet and what does not. The Red Pen showed why it matters even when a term sheet is non-binding: the vague words in draft 2 become the starting point for the binding agreement, and changing them later costs leverage.

Recap

Four models, each with an engine and a weak point. Rule 129: fund ambition with patient money. Three pockets, valued separately. Governance that makes conflicts visible. A waterfall you can work aloud. A committee pitch built on mechanisms rather than reassurance.

head: The six questions
speak: There are four ways to make money from buildings: build and sell, build and hold, develop with other people's capital for fees and promote, or use construction cash to fund development. Each has a weak point, and the best firms build their controls around it. Olympia and York shows what happens when a great developer funds long-life buildings with short money in a turning cycle. Rule 129: never copy an elite developer's ambition without its funding; match the term of every dollar to the time the asset needs, and hold liquidity to outlast a downturn. A developer is paid in three pockets: fees cover overhead, ownership builds wealth, and promote is never budgeted. Managing other people's money brings duties, so I disclose conflicts, test related-party contracts and agree removal terms early. And in any term sheet, I read the definitions behind the headline numbers, because they decide who gets paid.
terms: Term sheet — a summary of the main terms of a proposed deal, usually non-binding except for named clauses.
Fee base — the amount, such as project cost or equity, against which a percentage fee is calculated.
Alignment — the condition in which the sponsor's rewards rise and fall with the investor's results.

hostile.q: Your term sheet makes your affiliate the contractor on every project and leaves your co-investment optional. Why would we sign it?
hostile.a: You should not, and I will withdraw both clauses. The affiliate will bid like anyone else, with competing bids, a capped fee, audit rights and your written approval. My co-investment will be fixed at 10 percent of equity on your terms. I will also define the fee bases, state that the preferred return compounds, tie the promote to distributions above it and add a key-person clause, so the next draft protects you without my having to promise it.
